items.name: codebase-design
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules: improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable.
items.summary: codebase-design is a shared vocabulary reference for designing deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. It defines the terms module, interface, implementation, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, and locality, and insists on using them exactly instead of 'component', 'service', or 'boundary'. It carries design principles (the deletion test, the interface is the test surface, one adapter means a hypothetical seam) and testability rules like accepting dependencies rather than creating them. Companion files cover deepening a cluster given its dependencies (DEEPENING.md) and exploring alternative interfaces via parallel sub-agents (DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md). Reach for it when designing or restructuring a module's interface, deciding where a seam goes, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
highlights: Eight-term glossary used exactly: module, interface, implementation, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality
Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation; a module can have internal seams for its own tests
The deletion test: if deleting a module makes complexity reappear across N callers, it was earning its keep
One adapter means a hypothetical seam, two adapters means a real one; do not introduce a seam unless something varies ac
Testability rules: accept dependencies instead of creating them, return results instead of side effects, keep the surfac

items.name: diagnosing-bugs
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Get a systematic, step-by-step process that surfaces the real root cause instead of guessing at bugs.
items.summary: diagnosing-bugs is a six-phase discipline for hard bugs and performance regressions. Phase 1 is the core: build a tight, deterministic, agent-runnable feedback loop (one command that goes red on this exact bug) before any theorising; the doc lists ten ways to construct one, from failing tests and curl scripts to bisection harnesses and property/fuzz loops. Later phases reproduce and minimise the failure, generate 3-5 falsifiable ranked hypotheses, instrument one variable at a time with uniquely tagged debug logs, then write a regression test before the fix at a correct seam. Cleanup requires re-running the original repro, grepping out tagged instrumentation, and stating the winning hypothesis in the commit message. If the post-mortem shows no good test seam existed, the finding hands off to the improve-codebase-architecture skill.

Completion gate: one fast, deterministic, agent-runnable command, already run once, that goes red on the user's exact sy

Phase 3 requires 3-5 ranked falsifiable hypotheses shown to the user before testing any of them
Regression test is written before the fix, but only at a correct seam; a missing seam is itself the finding and hands of

items.name: code-review
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Reviews a branch or PR diff on two axes at once: conformance to coding standards plus a code-smell baseline, and whether it actually implements the original spec.
items.summary: code-review reviews the diff between HEAD and a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two independent axes: Standards (does the code follow the repo's documented coding standards plus a 12-smell Fowler baseline) and Spec (does it implement what the originating issue or PRD asked for). It pins the fixed point with a three-dot git diff, locates the spec via commit issue references or docs, gathers standards sources, then spawns two parallel sub-agents so the axes do not pollute each other's context. Findings are reported side by side under Standards and Spec headings, never merged or reranked, because a change can pass one axis and fail the other. Use it to review a branch, a PR, or work-in-progress changes against a fixed point.

items.name: wayfinder
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Breaks large, unclear work into typed investigation tickets on an issue tracker, building a shared map of decisions and open questions to resolve one at a time.
items.summary: wayfinder plans a chunk of work too big for one agent session by charting it as a shared map on the repo's issue tracker. Charting starts by naming the destination (a spec, a decision to lock, or an in-place change), then fans out breadth-first to create a map issue labeled wayfinder:map with child tickets, each a question sized to one 100K-token session and typed as research, prototype, grilling, or task. Blocking uses the tracker's native dependency links so the frontier of takeable tickets is visible in the tracker UI. A work session claims one frontier ticket, resolves it, posts the answer as a resolution comment, closes it, and appends a pointer to the map's Decisions-so-far index, graduating newly specifiable work out of the 'Not yet specified' fog. It plans rather than executes by default and never resolves more than one ticket per session. Developers reach for it when a loose idea spans many sessions and the route to done is not yet visible.

items.name: resolving-merge-conflicts
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Quickly understand, resolve, and commit merge conflicts without losing work or breaking their flow.
items.summary: resolving-merge-conflicts handles an in-progress git merge or rebase conflict in five steps. It first inspects the current state, git history, and conflicting files, then finds the primary sources for each conflict, reading commit messages, PRs, and original issues to understand why each change was made. Each hunk is resolved to preserve both intents where possible; where they are incompatible it picks the side matching the merge's stated goal and notes the trade-off, never inventing new behaviour and never aborting. It then discovers and runs the project's automated checks (typically typecheck, tests, format), fixes anything the merge broke, and finishes by staging, committing, and continuing a rebase until all commits are rebased. Developers reach for it whenever git stops mid-merge or mid-rebase with conflict markers.
